summary: Vocabulary/naming guidance for 9–11 year-olds on the major human organ systems. The teaching objective is PRODUCTIVE, precise use of technical terms (organ, organ system, circulatory, digestive, respiratory, skeletal, muscular, plus component terms nutrient, oxygen, carbon dioxide, blood vessel, artery, vein, capillary, enzyme), each anchored to a canonical image and a one-line function, with explicit work on predictably confused pairs (artery vs vein by direction; organ vs organ system as part vs team). Labelled-figure and matching activities build and check term→structure→function links; productive speaking/writing moves learners from recognition to independent use. This mostly consolidates vocabulary met across KS2 (Y3 nutrition and skeletal/muscular, Y4 digestive, Y6 circulatory); some terms such as enzyme and respiratory system go beyond KS2 statutory content and need a simple introduction.
misconceptions: Confusing artery and vein (thinking arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood, or muddling direction) rather than defining them by flow relative to the heart.
Using 'organ' and 'organ system' interchangeably, missing that a system is several organs working together.
Treating 'digestion', 'nutrient' and 'enzyme' as vague synonyms rather than distinct terms with precise meanings.
Thinking a technical term and an everyday word mean the same (e.g. 'vessel', 'tissue') and using loose synonyms.
Assigning a component term to the wrong system (e.g. placing 'enzyme' under circulatory) through weak organisation of vocabulary.

activities.title: Labelled body 'vocabulary map': one system at a time
steps: Reveal one organ system at a time (circulatory, digestive, respiratory, skeletal, or muscular) on a labelled body figure, so only the organs of that system are highlighted while the others are hidden.

Tap or point to any highlighted part to surface its exact name and a single precise one-line function sentence using the target term, e.g. 'the artery is a blood vessel that carries blood AWAY from the heart'.

Read the component terms where they appear as callouts: capillary (with artery and vein) on the circulatory system and enzyme on the digestive system, while nutrient, oxygen and carbon dioxide appear as callouts linking the systems they connect (e.g. oxygen on both the respiratory and circulatory systems), so each word is tied to the system or systems it belongs to.
Say aloud, for two systems, the name of each organ and what it does, using the exact technical term each time.
activities.insight: Each technical term names a specific structure or substance with a specific function or role. Some component terms belong to one system (arteries, veins and capillaries to the circulatory system; enzyme, in the sense of digestive enzymes, to the digestive system), while others (oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrient) link more than one system.

activities.title: Pin down the confusable pairs
steps: Place 'artery' and 'vein' side by side and state the main difference that distinguishes them: an artery carries blood AWAY from the heart; a vein carries blood back TO the heart.
Compare 'organ' and 'organ system' side by side and state that an organ (e.g. the heart) is one part, while an organ system is several organs working together.
Write or say one sentence for each pair that makes the contrast explicit (e.g. 'An artery carries blood away from the heart, but a vein carries blood back to it.').
activities.insight: Artery and vein differ by the DIRECTION of flow relative to the heart (not simply 'oxygen-rich vs not'); an organ is a single part and an organ system is a team of organs.

activities.title: Match, sort and complete to practise the terms
steps: Match each term to the correct organ/system and to its one-line function.

Sort the terms that have a single owning system in this topic under that system — artery, vein and capillary under circulatory; enzyme (here meaning digestive enzymes that break down food) under digestive. For terms that span systems (oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrient), name the systems they link rather than forcing one box.
Complete short sentences that require the exact term, e.g. 'The ___ carries blood away from the heart.'
Choose the correct term in a contrast item on artery vs vein and justify the choice by direction of flow.
activities.insight: The learner can select and place the precise term rather than a loose everyday synonym, and recognises that some terms link more than one system.

activities.title: Explain a running scenario in your own words
steps: Describe what happens in your body when you run for the bus, using these words as you go: respiratory system, circulatory system, artery, oxygen.
Say what each system is doing and how the two systems work together (breathing rate and heart rate both rise).
State how an artery differs from a vein, using the direction of blood flow relative to the heart.
Optionally, explain a body system to a listener who asks follow-up questions, so misused terms can be corrected in context (e.g. if 'vein' and 'artery' are swapped).
activities.insight: The learner can USE the vocabulary spontaneously and correctly in connected explanation, not merely recognise it — the real target of a language objective.

checkQuestion: Describe what happens in your body when you run for the bus, using these words as you go: respiratory system, circulatory system, artery, oxygen. Say what each system is doing, and how blood in an artery is different from blood in a vein.
checkAnswer: The child uses each term correctly: the respiratory system takes in oxygen (the lungs breathe faster); the circulatory system (heart and blood vessels) pumps blood faster to carry that oxygen to the muscles; arteries carry blood AWAY from the heart (usually oxygen-rich, under high pressure) while veins carry blood back TO the heart. Each term appears in a meaningful, correct sentence.
